newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland publishes secret texts of ex-PM spy probe.
newsitem.headline: Poland publishes secret texts of ex-PM spy probe.

text.p: Poland's government published on Monday a "White Book" said to contain all documents gathered in a probe of security service allegations that former prime minister Jozef Oleksy collaborated with Moscow spies.

The book had more than 450 pages of documents -- many stamped "secret" -- providing a mine of detail but at first sight adding little to widely-leaked outlines of the episode which rocked Poland early this year.
Oleksy, who proclaims his innocence, quit in January after military prosecutors decided to investigate the allegations.
The prosecutors dropped the inquiry in April, saying the evidence was clearly inadequate, and Oleksy now leads the ex-communists, the dominant party in the ruling coalition.

Justice Minister Leszek Kubicki told a news conference that all materials relating to the case were in the book, except for some names and details kept back to safeguard Polish intelligence and some filthy language cited in transcripts.
Where cuts had been made, they were marked and explained, while the obscenities used by Polish officers could be guessed as first letters of the words were provided.

The Oleksy affair erupted in December as Lech Walesa was about to hand over the presidency to ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski, who had won elections. Outgoing interior minister Andrzej Milczanowski, a Walesa ally, outlined the allegations to a stunned parliament.
But official reports later suggested that the evidence against Oleksy, partly from an alleged mole in Russian intelligence, contained major flaws and gaps.
Oleksy and his supporters said the accusations were cooked up by pro-Walesa officers for political reasons.
Milczanowski denies this, and told PAP news agency: "I consider my actions were justified, correct and accurate."

Walesa himself said that the publication of the White Book did not clear up the issue which would be settled after elections, due in September next year, when he hoped the opposition would be stronger in parliament.
"We will return to this issue when there is a more balanced parliament, and we will fully sort it out," the former Solidarity leader told PAP in his home town Gdansk.

The "White Book", issued to journalists and due to go on public sale on Tuesday, contained a critical internal report in May by the security service about the operation, which suggested political motives played a part in the gathering of evidence.

Interior Minister Zbigniew Siemiatkowski told the news conference that while Oleksy was clearly not the alleged Moscow spy, codenamed "Olin", in Poland's ruling circles, a hunt was still on to uncover any such agent.
The allegations against Oleksy centred on his contacts with Russian diplomat and intelligence officer Vladimir Alganov.
One theory was that Russian agents might have stirred up the rumpus to make Poland seem chaotic or riddled with spies and harm its bid to enter NATO, which Russia saw as a threat.

The security service report in the White Book also raised this idea. "Realisation of operational activities suggests that the threat of a provocation or inspiration from the Russian side was not adequately taken into account," it said.
